_about: The research behind the rating framework, and where Stephanie's judgment comes in. Rendered on /how-we-review (#research, #judgment) and summarized in the site footer. Every finding links to its source; keep it that way.
summary: Every score is built from public data and checked every month: user ratings 40%, popularity 25%, best-of lists 20% and value 15%. No one's opinion goes into a score, ours included, and no vendor can pay for a place. Stephanie's picks sit beside the scores, labeled as hers, and never change one.

research.finding: G2 places software on two measures, user satisfaction and market presence, and its Grid placement can't be changed by hand.
research.usedFor: Our user and popularity scores mirror those two measures, and no one can adjust a score or a rank by hand.

research.finding: Capterra's Shortlist scores each product half on user ratings from the last 12 months and half on popularity.
research.usedFor: Same two pillars. We weight users above popularity (40% to 25%) because popularity rewards whoever has been around longest.

research.finding: G2 counts a review about 3% less for every month it ages, and TrustRadius weights newer reviews more and gives extra weight to reviews collected independently of vendors.
research.usedFor: We re-check every rating monthly and count review growth in the popularity score. Lists published by companies that sell what they rank never count.
research.source: G2 research guidelines; TrustRadius scoring FAQ

research.finding: IMDb's published weighted rating pulls titles with few votes toward the overall average, so a handful of votes can't outrank thousands.
research.usedFor: Our users score uses the same adjustment: a tool with 37 reviews moves a little toward the category average; one with 3,200 barely moves. Below 25 reviews there is no score at all.

research.finding: Northwestern's Spiegel Research Center found purchase likelihood peaks at 4.2 to 4.5 stars and falls as ratings near a perfect 5, and that five reviews make a purchase 270% more likely than none.
research.usedFor: We always print the review count next to a rating, and when a tool has nothing but perfect scores, we look closer.

research.finding: Reviewers who get something in return rate the same products about 0.4 to 0.5 stars higher, and disclosing the incentive doesn't remove the bias.
research.usedFor: Where a source labels reviews as incentivized or vendor-invited, we record the share and show it next to the rating.
research.source: University of Florida, Warrington College of Business

research.finding: Consumer Reports builds its overall scores from tests and owner surveys, and a product earns its Recommended label through those scores.
research.usedFor: Our labels like Top-rated checker and Small teams pick are earned the same way: they go to the top data score in their group, automatically.

research.finding: Wirecutter's picks are editorial judgments, kept independent of affiliate deals and advertising.
research.usedFor: Stephanie's picks work like Wirecutter's: a named person's judgment, labeled as hers, and kept apart from the scores.

does: Name my picks: an up-and-coming pick for job seekers and a top pick for hiring teams, labeled as mine.
Nominate tools to check, so a good one doesn't have to wait for a marketing budget to get noticed.
Write the guidance: what a recruiter sees when your resume lands, how to use a tool and what to watch out for.
never: Move a tool up or down a ranking.
Change a weight for one tool or one category.
Accept money, gifts or deals for any of the above.

limits: Most sources publish an average rating, not each review's date, so we can't yet discount older reviews the way G2 does. Where a source offers a last-12-months rating, we use it.
Independent lists for applicant tracking systems aren't tracked yet, so those scores use user ratings, popularity and value, which share the best-of lists weight.
